title: IV. A Hymn And A Secret
paragraphs: It was quite late when Alyosha rang at the prison gate. Days are short in November, and dusk was already coming on. But Alyosha knew he would be let in without trouble. Our little town handled such things the way every town does. At first, once the preliminary inquiry was over, relatives and a few other people could see Mitya only after going through certain unavoidable formalities. Later the formalities stayed in place, but exceptions were made for some of Mitya’s visitors, at least. In fact, the meetings with the prisoner in the room set aside for them were sometimes practically _tête-à-tête_.

These exceptions were few, though. Only Grushenka, Alyosha and Rakitin were treated this way. The police captain, Mihail Mihailovitch, was very favorably inclined toward Grushenka. The way he had abused her at Mokroe lay heavy on the old man’s conscience, and when he learned the whole story he changed his opinion of her entirely. And strange to say, he was firmly convinced of Mitya’s guilt, yet once Mitya was in prison the old man judged him more and more mildly. “Perhaps he was a good-hearted man,” he thought, “who came to grief through drink and dissipation.” His first horror had turned into pity. As for Alyosha, the captain was very fond of him and had known him for a long time. Rakitin had recently begun visiting the prisoner very often. He was one of the closest acquaintances of “the police captain’s young ladies,” as the captain called them, and was always hanging about their house. He also gave lessons at the house of the prison superintendent. The superintendent was strict in carrying out his duties, but he was a kind old man. Alyosha had known him well for years, and the old man liked talking with him, usually about sacred subjects. He respected Ivan Fyodorovitch and stood in awe of his opinion, though he was a great philosopher himself, “self-taught,” of course. But Alyosha drew him irresistibly. This past year the old man had started studying the Apocryphal Gospels, and he was forever discussing his impressions with his young friend. He used to visit Alyosha at the monastery and talk for hours with him and with the monks. So even when Alyosha came late to the prison, he only had to go to the superintendent and everything was made easy. Besides, everyone in the prison, down to the lowliest warder, had grown used to Alyosha. And the sentry, naturally, gave him no trouble so long as the authorities were satisfied.

When Mitya was called from his cell, he always came down to the place set aside for interviews. As Alyosha entered the room, he found Rakitin just taking his leave of Mitya. Both were talking loudly. Mitya was laughing heartily as he saw Rakitin out, while Rakitin seemed to be grumbling. Rakitin did not like meeting Alyosha, especially lately. He hardly spoke to him and gave him a stiff bow. Seeing Alyosha come in, he frowned and looked away, as if he were completely taken up with buttoning his big, warm, fur-trimmed overcoat. Then he began hunting at once for his umbrella.
“I’d better be careful not to forget my things,” he muttered, just to say something.
“And be careful not to forget other people’s things,” said Mitya as a joke, and laughed right away at his own wit. Rakitin flared up at once.
“Save that advice for your own family, a slave-driving bunch if there ever was one, and don’t give it to Rakitin,” he cried, suddenly shaking with rage.

“What’s the matter? I was joking!” cried Mitya. “Damn it all! They’re all like that,” he said to Alyosha, nodding toward Rakitin’s fast-retreating back. “He sat here laughing and cheerful, and all at once he boils over like that. He didn’t even nod to you. Have you broken with him completely? And why are you so late? I haven’t just been waiting for you, I’ve been thirsting for you the whole morning. But never mind. We’ll make up for it now.”
“Why does he come here so often? You can’t be such great friends,” said Alyosha. He, too, nodded at the door where Rakitin had gone out.

“Great friends with Rakitin? No, not that much. Could I be, with a pig like that? He thinks I’m ... a blackguard. And they can’t take a joke, either. That’s the worst thing about people like him. They never understand a joke, and their souls are dry, dry and flat. They remind me of the prison walls the day I was first brought here. But he’s a clever fellow, very clever. Well, Alexey, it’s all over with me now.”
He sat down on the bench and made Alyosha sit beside him.
“Yes, the trial’s tomorrow. Are you so without hope, brother?” Alyosha said, uneasy at heart.

“What are you talking about?” said Mitya, giving him a rather uncertain look. “Oh, the trial, you mean! Damn it all! Up to now we’ve talked only about things that don’t matter, about this trial, and I haven’t said a word to you about the main thing. Yes, the trial is tomorrow. But it wasn’t the trial I meant when I said it was all over with me. Why are you looking at me so critically?”
“What do you mean, Mitya?”
“Ideas, ideas, nothing but ideas! Ethics! What is ethics?”
“Ethics?” Alyosha asked, puzzled.
“Yes. Is it a science?”
“Yes, there is such a science ... but ... to tell the truth, I can’t explain to you what kind of science it is.”

“Rakitin knows. Rakitin knows plenty, damn him! He’s not going to be a monk. He means to go to Petersburg. There he’ll take up criticism with an uplifting tendency. Who knows, he may be useful and make a career for himself, too. Ough! They’re first-rate at making careers, these people! Damn ethics, I’m done for, Alexey, I am, you man of God! I love you more than anyone. My heart aches just looking at you. Who was Karl Bernard?”
“Karl Bernard?” Alyosha was surprised again.
“No, not Karl. Wait, I got it wrong. Claude Bernard. What was he? A chemist, or what?”
“He must be a scholar,” Alyosha answered. “But I can’t tell you much about him either. I’ve heard of him as a scholar, but I don’t know what kind.”

“Well, the hell with him, then! I don’t know either,” swore Mitya. “A scoundrel of some sort, most likely. They’re all scoundrels. And Rakitin will make his way. Rakitin will get on anywhere; he’s another Bernard. Ugh, these Bernards! They’re everywhere.”
“But what’s wrong?” Alyosha pressed him.

“He wants to write an article about me, about my case, and start his literary career with it. That’s why he comes; he said so himself. He wants to prove some theory. He wants to say, ‘He couldn’t help murdering his father; he was corrupted by his environment,’ and so on. He explained it all to me. He’s going to add a tinge of Socialism, he says. But damn the fellow, he can add a tinge if he likes, I don’t care. He can’t bear Ivan, he hates him. He’s not fond of you, either. But I don’t throw him out, because he’s a clever fellow. Awfully conceited, though. I told him just now, ‘The Karamazovs aren’t blackguards but philosophers, because all true Russians are philosophers. And though you’ve studied, you’re no philosopher—you’re a low fellow.’ He laughed, so spitefully. And I said to him, ‘_De ideabus non est disputandum_.’ Not bad, eh? You see, I can pass myself off as a classicist!” Mitya suddenly laughed.
“Why is it all over with you? You said so a minute ago,” Alyosha put in.
“Why is it all over with me? H’m!... The thing is ... when you take it all together, I’m sorry to lose God. That’s why.”
“What do you mean, ‘sorry to lose God’?”

“Imagine this: inside, in the nerves, in the head—that is, these nerves are there in the brain ... (damn them!) there are sort of little tails, the little tails of those nerves, and the moment they start quivering ... that is, you see, I look at something with my eyes, and then they start quivering, those little tails ... and when they quiver, an image appears ... it doesn’t appear at once, but an instant goes by, a second ... and then something like a moment appears; that is, not a moment—devil take the moment!—but an image; that is, an object, or an action, damn it! That’s why I see and then think, because of those tails, and not at all because I have a soul, or because I’m some kind of image and likeness. All that is nonsense! Rakitin explained it all to me yesterday, brother, and it simply knocked me flat. It’s magnificent, Alyosha, this science! A new man is arising—that I understand.... And yet I’m sorry to lose God!”
“Well, that at least is a good thing,” said Alyosha.

“That I’m sorry to lose God? It’s chemistry, brother, chemistry! Nothing to be done about it, your reverence, you’ll have to move over and make room for chemistry. And Rakitin certainly dislikes God. Ough! Doesn’t he dislike Him! That’s the sore point with all of them. But they hide it. They lie. They pretend. ‘Will you preach this in your reviews?’ I asked him. ‘Oh, if I did it openly, they wouldn’t let it through,’ he said. He laughed. ‘But what will become of men then,’ I asked him, ‘without God and immortal life? All things are lawful then, they can do what they like?’ ‘Didn’t you know that?’ he said, laughing. ‘A clever man can do what he likes,’ he said. ‘A clever man knows his way around. But you put your foot in it by committing a murder, and now you’re rotting in prison.’ He says that to my face! A regular pig! I used to kick such people out, and now I listen to them. He talks a lot of sense, too. Writes well. Last week he started reading me an article of his. I copied out three lines of it. Wait a minute. Here it is.”
Mitya hurriedly pulled a scrap of paper from his pocket and read:
“‘To settle this question, it is above all essential to put one’s personality in contradiction with one’s reality.’ Do you understand that?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha. He looked at Mitya and listened to him with curiosity.

“Neither do I. It’s murky and obscure, but intellectual. ‘Everybody writes like that now,’ he says, ‘it’s the effect of their environment.’ They’re afraid of the environment. He writes poetry, too, the rascal. He’s written some in honor of Madame Hohlakov’s foot. Ha ha ha!”
“I’ve heard about that,” said Alyosha.
“You have? And have you heard the poem?”
“No.”

“I’ve got it. Here it is. I’ll read it to you. You don’t know this—I haven’t told you—there’s quite a story behind it. He’s a rascal! Three weeks ago he started teasing me. ‘You’ve landed yourself in a mess, like a fool, over three thousand, but I’m going to grab a hundred and fifty thousand. I’m going to marry a widow and buy a house in Petersburg.’ And he told me he was courting Madame Hohlakov. She never had much brains, even in her youth, and now at forty she’s lost what she had. ‘But she’s awfully sentimental,’ he says. ‘That’s how I’ll get her. When I’ve married her, I’ll take her to Petersburg and start a newspaper there.’ And his mouth was simply watering, the beast, and not for the widow but for the hundred and fifty thousand. He made me believe it, too. He came to see me every day. ‘She’s coming round,’ he told me, beaming with delight. And then, all of a sudden, he was thrown out of the house. Perhotin’s carrying everything before him, bravo! I could kiss the silly old noodle for throwing him out. And Rakitin had already written this doggerel. ‘It’s the first time I’ve dirtied my hands writing poetry,’ he said. ‘It’s to win her heart, so it’s for a good cause. Once I’ve got hold of the silly woman’s fortune, I can be of great social use.’ They always have this social excuse for every nasty thing they do! ‘At any rate, it’s better than your Pushkin’s poetry,’ he said, ‘because I’ve managed to preach enlightenment even in that.’ I understand what he means about Pushkin, I quite see it, if Pushkin really was a man of talent and wrote only about women’s feet. But wasn’t Rakitin puffed up about his doggerel! The vanity of these fellows! ‘On the Recovery of the Swollen Foot of the Object of My Affections’—that’s the title he came up with. He’s a waggish fellow.
A captivating little foot, Though swollen and red and tender! The doctors come and plasters put, But still they cannot mend her.
Yet it’s not for her foot I dread— A theme for Pushkin’s muse more fit— It’s not her foot, it is her head: I tremble for her loss of wit!
For as her foot swells, strange to say, Her intellect is on the wane— Oh, for some remedy I pray That may restore both foot and brain!
He’s a pig, a regular pig, but he’s a sly one, the rascal! And he really has managed to slip in a progressive idea. And wasn’t he furious when she kicked him out! He ground his teeth!”
“He’s taken his revenge already,” said Alyosha. “He’s written a paragraph about Madame Hohlakov.”
And Alyosha told him briefly about the paragraph in _Gossip_.

“That’s his work, that’s his work!” Mitya agreed, frowning. “That’s him! These paragraphs ... I know them ... the insulting things that have been written about Grushenka, for instance.... And about Katya, too.... H’m!”
He crossed the room with a tormented air.

“Brother, I can’t stay long,” Alyosha said after a pause. “Tomorrow will be a great and terrible day for you. The judgment of God will be carried out ... and I’m amazed at you. You walk about here, talking about I don’t know what ...”

“No, don’t be amazed at me,” Mitya broke in warmly. “Am I supposed to talk about that stinking dog? About the murderer? We’ve talked enough about him. I don’t want to say another word about the stinking son of Stinking Lizaveta! God will kill him, you’ll see. Hush!”
He went up to Alyosha in excitement and kissed him. His eyes glowed.

“Rakitin wouldn’t understand this,” he began in a kind of exaltation. “But you, you’ll understand it all. That’s why I was thirsting for you. You see, there’s so much I’ve wanted to tell you for ever so long, here, inside these peeling walls. But I haven’t said a word about what matters most. The moment never seemed to come. Now I can’t wait any longer. I have to pour my heart out to you. Brother, in these last two months I’ve found a new man in myself. A new man has risen up in me. He was hidden inside me, and he would never have come to the surface if it hadn’t been for this blow from heaven. I’m afraid! And what do I care if I spend twenty years in the mines, breaking ore with a hammer? I’m not afraid of that at all. It’s something else I’m afraid of now: that the new man may leave me. Even there, in the mines, underground, I may find a human heart in another convict and murderer next to me, and I may make friends with him. Even there a man can live and love and suffer. You can thaw and revive a frozen heart in that convict, you can wait on him for years, and at last bring up from the dark depths a lofty soul, a feeling, suffering creature. You can bring forth an angel, create a hero! There are so many of them, hundreds of them, and we’re all to blame for them. Why did I dream of that ‘babe’ at such a moment? ‘Why is the babe so poor?’ That was a sign to me at that moment. It’s for the babe that I’m going. Because we’re all responsible for all. For all the ‘babes,’ because there are big children as well as little children. All are ‘babes.’ I go for all, because someone has to go for all. I didn’t kill father, but I have to go. I accept it. It all came to me here, here, inside these peeling walls. There are masses of them down there, hundreds of them underground, with hammers in their hands. Oh, yes, we’ll be in chains and there’ll be no freedom, but then, in our great sorrow, we’ll rise again to joy, without which man cannot live nor God exist, for God gives joy: it’s His privilege—a grand one. Ah, man should be dissolved in prayer! What would I be down there underground without God? Rakitin’s laughing! If they drive God from the earth, we’ll shelter Him underground. A man can’t exist in prison without God; it’s even more impossible than outside prison. And then we men underground will sing out of the bowels of the earth a glorious hymn to God, with Whom is joy. Hail to God and His joy! I love Him!”
Mitya was fighting for breath as this wild speech burst out of him. He had turned white, his lips shook, and tears ran down his face.

“Yes, life is full. There’s life even underground,” he started again. “You won’t believe it, Alexey, but how I want to live now! Inside these peeling walls a hunger for existence and awareness has come over me. Rakitin can’t grasp that. All he wants is to build a house and rent out apartments. But you, I’ve been longing for you. And what is suffering anyway? I’m not afraid of it, even if there were no end to it. I’m not afraid of it now. I was before. Do you know, maybe I won’t answer at the trial at all.... And I seem to have such strength in me now that I think I could bear anything, any pain at all, as long as I can say it to myself every moment: ‘I exist.’ In a thousand agonies—I exist. Stretched on the rack—I exist! Though I sit alone on top of a pillar—I exist! I see the sun, and if I can’t see the sun, I know it’s there. And a whole life lies in that, in knowing the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are the death of me. Damn them! Brother Ivan—”
“What about Ivan?” Alyosha broke in, but Mitya didn’t hear.

“You see, I never had any of these doubts before. They were buried in me. Maybe it was exactly because ideas I couldn’t understand were boiling up inside me that I drank and brawled and raged. I wanted to choke them down, quiet them, smother them. Ivan isn’t Rakitin. There’s an idea in him. Ivan is a sphinx, and he says nothing. He’s always silent. It’s God who worries me. Nothing else worries me but that. What if He doesn’t exist? What if Rakitin is right and God is only an idea men invented? Then, without Him, man is lord of the earth and of the whole universe. Magnificent! Only how is man going to be good without God? That’s the question. I keep coming back to it. Who will man love, then? Who will he thank? Who will he sing the hymn to? Rakitin laughs. Rakitin says you can love humanity without God. Well, only a sniveling idiot could say so. I can’t make sense of it. Life’s easy for Rakitin. ‘Better think about extending civil rights, or about holding down the price of meat. That’s a simpler, more direct way to show your love for humanity than philosophy.’ And I told him, ‘Well, you without a God are the very man who’d raise the price of meat, if it suited you, and squeeze a rouble out of every kopeck.’ He lost his temper. But after all, what is goodness? Answer me that, Alexey. Goodness is one thing to me and another to a Chinese man, so it’s relative. Or isn’t it? Isn’t it relative? A treacherous question! Don’t laugh when I tell you it’s kept me awake two nights. What amazes me now is that people can go on living and never give it a thought. Vanity! Ivan has no God. He has an idea. It’s beyond me. But he says nothing. I think he must be a Freemason. I asked him, and he said nothing. I wanted to drink from the springs of his soul—and he was silent. Only once did he let a word slip.”
“What did he say?” Alyosha asked at once.

“I said to him, ‘So everything is lawful, if that’s the case?’ He frowned. ‘Fyodor Pavlovitch, our papa,’ he said, ‘was a pig, but his ideas were sound enough.’ That’s what slipped out of him, and that’s all he said. That beats Rakitin by a mile.”
“Yes,” Alyosha agreed bitterly. “When was he here?”

“Later, I’ll tell you that later. Now I have to talk about something else. I haven’t told you anything about Ivan till now. I kept it for last. When all this is over here and the verdict is in, then I’ll tell you something. I’ll tell you everything. There’s something tremendous between us.... And you will be my judge in it. But don’t start on that now. Keep quiet. You talk about tomorrow, about the trial, but would you believe it, I know nothing about it.”
“Have you spoken with your lawyer?”

“What good is a lawyer? I told him the whole story. He’s a soft, city-bred rogue—a Bernard! And he doesn’t believe me, not a bit. Imagine, he thinks I did it. I can see it. ‘In that case,’ I asked him, ‘why did you come to defend me?’ Hang the lot of them! They’ve even brought in a doctor to prove I’m mad. I won’t stand for that! And Katerina Ivanovna means to do her ‘duty’ to the end, whatever it costs her!” Mitya smiled bitterly. “That cat! That hard-hearted creature! She knows I said at Mokroe that she was a woman of ‘great wrath.’ It was repeated to her. Yes, the facts against me now are as many as the sands of the sea. Grigory holds to his story. Grigory is honest, but a fool. Plenty of people are honest because they’re fools. That’s Rakitin’s notion. Grigory is my enemy. And some people are worth more as enemies than as friends. I mean Katerina Ivanovna. I’m afraid, oh, I’m afraid she’ll tell about how she bowed down to the ground over that four thousand. She’ll pay it back to the last farthing. I don’t want her sacrifice. They’ll shame me at the trial. I wonder how I’ll bear it. Go to her, Alyosha, and ask her not to bring that up in court. Can you do that? But the devil take it, it doesn’t matter! I’ll get through somehow. I don’t pity her. She’s done it to herself. She’s earned what she gets. I’ll have my own story to tell, Alexey.” He smiled bitterly again. “Only ... only Grusha, Grusha! Good Lord! Why must she suffer like this?” he cried out suddenly, in tears. “Grusha is killing me. Just thinking of her is killing me, killing me. She was with me a little while ago....”
“She told me you hurt her badly today.”
“I know. Damn my temper! It was jealousy. I was sorry. I kissed her when she left. But I didn’t ask her to forgive me.”
“Why didn’t you?” Alyosha cried.
All at once Mitya laughed, almost cheerfully.

“May God spare you, my dear boy, from ever asking pardon for some fault from a woman you love. Above all from a woman you love, however badly you were in the wrong. Because a woman—who the devil can make out a woman? I know a little about them, at least. But just try owning up to a woman that you’re at fault. Say, ‘I’m sorry, forgive me,’ and the reproaches come down like rain! She won’t simply and plainly forgive you, not for anything. She’ll grind you into the dust, haul out things that never happened, call up everything, forget nothing, add some of her own, and only then forgive you. And even the best of them, the very best, do this. She’ll scrape together every last scrap and pile it on your head. They’d skin you alive, I tell you, every one of them, these angels we can’t live without! I say it plainly and openly, dear boy: every decent man ought to be under some woman’s thumb. That’s my conviction—no, not conviction, my feeling. A man should be magnanimous, and there’s no disgrace in it for him! No disgrace for a hero, not even for a Cæsar! But all the same, never beg her pardon for anything. Remember that rule from your brother Mitya, who’s been ruined by women. No, I’d better make it up to Grusha some other way, without begging pardon. I worship her, Alexey, I worship her. Only she doesn’t see it. No, she still thinks I don’t love her enough. And she tortures me, tortures me with her love. The past was nothing! Back then it was only those infernal curves of hers that tortured me. But now I’ve taken her whole soul into mine, and through her I’ve become a man myself. Will they let us marry? If they don’t, I’ll die of jealousy. Every day I imagine something.... What did she say to you about me?”
Alyosha told him everything Grushenka had said to him that day. Mitya listened, made him go over certain things again, and seemed pleased.

“So she isn’t angry that I’m jealous?” he cried. “There’s a woman for you! ‘I’ve a fierce heart myself!’ Ah, I love such fierce hearts, though I can’t stand anyone being jealous of me. I can’t take it. We’ll fight. But I’ll love her, I’ll love her without end. Will they let us marry? Do they let convicts marry? That’s the question. And I can’t exist without her....”
Mitya crossed the room with a frown. It was nearly dark. All at once he seemed terribly uneasy.

“So there’s a secret, she says, a secret? We’ve hatched a plot against her, and Katya’s in it, she thinks. No, my good Grushenka, that’s not it. You’re far off the mark, with your silly woman’s ideas. Alyosha, darling, well, here goes! I’ll tell you our secret!”

He glanced around, stepped quickly up to Alyosha, who was standing in front of him, and whispered with an air of mystery, though in truth no one could hear them. The old warder was dozing in his corner, and not a word could reach the soldiers on guard.

“I’ll tell you our whole secret,” Mitya whispered in a rush. “I meant to tell you later. How could I decide anything without you? You’re everything to me. I say Ivan is above us, but you are my angel. Your decision will be the one that settles it. Maybe it’s you who are above us and not Ivan. You see, it’s a matter of conscience, of the higher conscience—the secret is so important I can’t settle it myself, and I’ve held it back until I could talk to you. Still, it’s too early to decide now, since we have to wait for the verdict. The moment the verdict comes, you’ll decide my fate. Don’t decide now. I’ll tell you now. You listen, but don’t decide. Stand there and keep still. I won’t tell you all of it. I’ll just give you the idea, no details, and you keep still. No questions, no moving. Agreed? But good heavens, what am I going to do about your eyes? I’m afraid your eyes will tell me your decision even if you say nothing. Oh! I’m afraid! Alyosha, listen! Ivan proposes that I _escape_. I won’t give you the details. It’s all been thought through, it can all be arranged. Hush, don’t decide. I’d go to America with Grusha. You know I can’t live without Grusha! What if they won’t let her follow me to Siberia? Do they let convicts get married? Ivan thinks not. And without Grusha, what would I do down there underground with a hammer? I’d only smash my own skull with the hammer! But then, on the other side, there’s my conscience. I’d have run away from suffering. A sign has come, and I’m refusing the sign. There’s a way of salvation open to me, and I’m turning my back on it. Ivan says that in America, ‘with the good will,’ I could do more good than underground. But what becomes of our hymn from underground? What is America? America is vanity again! And I expect there’s plenty of swindling in America too. I’d have run away from crucifixion! I’m telling you, Alexey, because you’re the only one who can understand this. There’s no one else. To everyone else it’s folly, madness, everything I’ve told you about the hymn. They’ll say I’ve lost my mind or I’m a fool. I haven’t lost my mind and I’m not a fool. Ivan understands about the hymn too. He understands, only he won’t answer—he won’t speak. He doesn’t believe in the hymn. Don’t speak, don’t speak. I can see how you look! You’ve decided already. Don’t decide, spare me! I can’t live without Grusha. Wait till after the trial!”
Mitya finished, beside himself. He gripped Alyosha’s shoulders with both hands, and his feverish, yearning eyes were fixed on his brother’s.
“They don’t let convicts marry, do they?” he asked a third time, in a begging voice.
Alyosha had listened in great astonishment, and he was deeply moved.
“Tell me one thing,” he said. “Is Ivan very set on this, and whose idea was it?”

“His, his, and he’s very set on it. At first he didn’t come to see me. Then suddenly he turned up a week ago and started in on it right away. He’s dead set on it. He doesn’t ask me, he orders me to escape. He has no doubt I’ll obey him, though I opened my whole heart to him as I have to you, and told him about the hymn too. He told me he’d arrange it. He’s found out everything. But more of that later. He’s just fixed on it. It all comes down to money: he’ll pay ten thousand for the escape and give me twenty thousand for America. And he says a magnificent escape can be arranged for ten thousand.”
“And he told you not to tell me, on any account?” Alyosha asked again.

“Not to tell anyone, and above all not you. Not to tell you on any account. No doubt he’s afraid you’ll stand in front of me as my conscience. Don’t tell him I told you. Don’t tell him, whatever happens.”
“You’re right,” said Alyosha. “It’s impossible to decide anything before the trial is over. After the trial you’ll decide for yourself. Then you’ll find that new man in you, and he will decide.”
“A new man, or a Bernard who’ll decide _à la_ Bernard, because I think I’m a contemptible Bernard myself,” said Mitya, with a bitter grin.
“But brother, do you have no hope at all of being acquitted?”

Mitya shrugged nervously and shook his head. “Alyosha, darling, it’s time you went,” he said, suddenly hurrying. “I hear the superintendent shouting in the yard. He’ll be in here any minute. We’re late, it’s against the rules. Embrace me quickly. Kiss me! Make the sign of the cross over me, darling, for the cross I have to carry tomorrow.”
They embraced and kissed.
“Ivan,” Mitya said suddenly, “proposes that I escape. But of course he believes I did it.”
A sorrowful smile crossed his lips.
“Did you ask him whether he believes it?” asked Alyosha.
“No, I didn’t. I wanted to, but I couldn’t. I hadn’t the nerve. But I saw it in his eyes. Well, good-by!”
They kissed again in a hurry, and Alyosha was already on his way out when Mitya suddenly called him back.

“Stand facing me! There, like that!” And once more he grabbed Alyosha, with both hands on his shoulders. His face went white all at once, so white that it showed dreadfully even in the failing light. His lips twitched, and his eyes bored into Alyosha.
“Alyosha, tell me the whole truth, as if you stood before God. Do you believe I did it? Do you, do you yourself, believe it? The whole truth, don’t lie!” he cried in desperation.
Everything seemed to heave and sway before Alyosha, and he felt something like a knife go into his heart.
“Hush! What are you saying?” he stammered helplessly.
“The whole truth, all of it, don’t lie!” Mitya repeated.
“Not for one moment have I believed you were the murderer!” The words came in a shaking voice from deep in Alyosha’s chest, and he raised his right hand into the air as though calling God to witness.
Mitya’s whole face shone with joy.

“Thank you!” he said slowly, like a man breathing out after a faint. “You’ve given me new life now. Would you believe it, until this moment I was afraid to ask you, you, even you. Well, go! You’ve given me strength for tomorrow. God bless you! Come on, go! Love Ivan!” Those were Mitya’s last words.

Alyosha left in tears. Mitya’s mistrust, his lack of faith even in him, in Alyosha—all of it suddenly opened up to Alyosha a depth of hopeless grief and despair in his unhappy brother’s soul that he had never suspected. Intense, endless pity swept over him at once. His torn heart ached sharply. “Love Ivan!”—he suddenly remembered Mitya’s words. And he was on his way to Ivan. He had badly wanted to see Ivan all day. He worried about Ivan as much as about Mitya, and now more than ever.
